question.problem:
Suppose we have a dataset consisting of $4$ datapoints with $2$ features in the form of the $4\times 2$ matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-0.33 & 1.18 \\ -0.49 & -0.88 \\ 1.49 & 0.48 \\ -0.66 & -0.77\end{aligned}]
$$

where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$).
We are also given the SVD decomposition $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ where:

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =[\begin{aligned}0.29 & 0.813 & 0.505 & 0.021 \\ -0.469 & -0.212 & 0.634 & -0.578 \\ 0.676 & -0.54 & 0.473 & 0.168 \\ -0.49 & -0.061 & 0.345 & 0.798\end{aligned}] \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.065 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.316 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.709 & -0.705 \\ 0.705 & 0.709\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following matrices corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance?

I. $[\begin{aligned}0.709 \\ 0.705\end{aligned}]$

II. $[\begin{aligned}-0.33 & 1.18 \\ -0.49 & -0.88 \\ 1.49 & 0.48 \\ -0.66 & -0.77\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.709 \\ 0.705\end{aligned}]$

III. $[\begin{aligned}0.29 \\ -0.469 \\ 0.676 \\ -0.49\end{aligned}]\cdot 2.065$
question.worked_solution:
The one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance is the projection onto the first principal component.

Recall that the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix ${X}^{T}X.$

Using the SVD and the fact that $U$ is orthogonal (i.e., ${U}^{T}U=I$), we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}^{T}X & =(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T}UΣ{V}^{T} \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}Σ{V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $Σ$ is a diagonal matrix, and so is ${Σ}^{T}Σ,$ we know that the eigenvectors of ${X}^{T}X$ are the columns of $V.$

In particular, the first principal component is the eigenvector of ${X}^{T}X$ corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. 
And since $Σ$ contains the corresponding singular values (square roots of the eigenvalues) in decreasing order, the first principal component is ${v}_{1},$ the first column of $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Option I represents ${v}_{1},$ which is the first principal component. It represents a direction in feature space, not a version of the data. Notice that it is also dimensionally incorrect, since it is a $2\times 1$ matrix instead of $4\times 1.$

- Option II corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance. Indeed, it represents $X\cdot {v}_{1},$ which is exactly the projection of $X$ onto the first principal component.

- Option III corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance. Notice that it represents ${u}_{1}\cdot {\sigma }_{1},$ where ${u}_{1}$ is the first column of $U$ and ${\sigma }_{1}$ is the first singular value. But this equals  $X\cdot {v}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X\cdot {v}_{1} & =UΣ{V}^{T}\cdot {v}_{1}=UΣ\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=U\cdot [\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]={u}_{1}\cdot {\sigma }_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
